quote: between the third hour and dawn
note: A roundabout way of telling the time. The day's hours were counted from sunrise, about six o'clock, so the third hour ended at about nine. As much of the sun's path is left as it covers in those first three hours: it is three hours before sunset, about three in the afternoon.
The sphere of heaven that carries the sun, never still, like a child at play. Exactly which circle of the sky Dante means is debated.

"There" is Purgatory, where the last quarter of the day, called vespers, was beginning. "Here" is Italy, where Dante sits writing. In his geography Purgatory is on the far side of the globe from Jerusalem, and Italy lies a quarter of the way round, so the clocks differ by nine hours.
The travelers began the climb on the eastern side of the mountain. Circling to the right, they have come far enough round its northern face to walk straight toward the setting sun.

quote: a brilliance far greater than before
note: A second light added to the sun's: the angel of this terrace, coming toward them.

quote: rising at the same angle it descended
note: The law of reflection: a ray of light leaves a mirror at the same angle at which it struck. Dante states it as a student of optics would.

quote: as a falling stone would drop
note: The line of a falling stone is the vertical, the plumb line. The ray coming down and the ray going up lean away from it by equal amounts, one on each side.
Observation and the science of optics, which was studied in the universities as part of the mathematics of light.
The angels. Dante's eyes are not yet strong enough for them. As he is cleansed, the same light will become a pleasure.

quote: far less steep than the others
note: Each stair is easier than the last, as the weight of sin comes off. The angel wipes the second P from Dante's forehead here, though the poem does not show it: Virgil mentions it a little later.

The fifth Beatitude, from the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:7), sung in Latin: Beati misericordes. Mercy is envy's opposite. The envious are pained by another's good fortune, the merciful by another's misfortune.
Sung in Italian. The source is uncertain. It may echo the close of the Beatitudes, "Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven" (Matthew 5:12).

context: In Canto 14 he cried out against people who set their hearts on things that cannot be shared. Dante has been turning the phrase over ever since.

quote: sharing means each person gets less
note: Money, land and honors are divided when shared, so every new owner leaves less for the others. Fear of losing one's share is the root of envy.

context: Virgil's remedy for envy: want what is found there. The goods of Heaven grow when they are shared.

note: Heaven pictured as a monastery, where the monks own nothing privately and say "ours" of everything.
Dante is still thinking of material things, so a true statement only confuses him more.

quote: like sunlight streaming to a clear surface
note: The heart of the canto. God's goodness goes out to souls as light goes to a bright body: the more the surface can take, the more it receives. A soul receives as much of God as it has love.

Each loving soul reflects what it receives onto the others. So every soul added to Heaven increases the joy of all the rest, the reverse of what happens with goods on earth. Paradiso shows this at length.

context: Virgil knows the limits of his own explanation. He stands for what human reason can reach. Beatrice, who waits at the top of the mountain, will speak with the knowledge of Heaven.

note: The P's cut into Dante's forehead at the gate, one for each deadly sin (Canto 9). Two are gone, pride and envy. Five remain: wrath, sloth, avarice, gluttony and lust.

quote: through the pain of feeling them
note: Sorrow for sin is itself the cure. The wounds close as the penitent feels them.
The third terrace, where wrath is purged. Its examples of the opposite virtue, gentleness, come neither as carvings nor as voices, but as visions inside Dante's mind.
The Temple in Jerusalem. At twelve, Jesus stayed behind there after a festival, and his parents searched three days before finding him among the teachers (Luke 2:41–50).

context: The first example of gentleness. After three days of fear she speaks to her son without anger. Her words are almost exactly those of the Gospel (Luke 2:48).

note: The wife of Pisistratus. A young man in love with their daughter had kissed the girl in public, and the mother wanted him put to death. The story comes from the Roman writer Valerius Maximus.
Athens. In the myth, Neptune and Minerva (the Greek Athena) both claimed the right to name the city. Minerva won by giving it the olive tree. Ovid tells the story in the Metamorphoses.
Athens as the home of philosophy and the arts, the school of the ancient world.
Ruler of Athens in the sixth century BC. He had seized power by force, but was remembered as a mild and able ruler. His answer is the classical example of gentleness.

Saint Stephen, the first Christian martyr, stoned to death outside Jerusalem. As he died he prayed, "Lord, do not hold this sin against them" (Acts 7:54–60). The Bible does not give his age: making him a youth is Dante's touch.
In Acts, Stephen looks up as the stoning begins and sees the heavens opened and the glory of God.
Dante's Italian has a famous paradox here: "my not false errors". The visions were errors, since nothing he saw was in front of him, but they were not false, since what they showed was true.
Dante's Italian says half a league, a longer distance. He has walked all that way in a trance, stumbling like a drunk.
Virgil can read Dante's thoughts, as he has shown many times since Hell. He has seen the visions too.
Gentleness and forgiveness, which put out the fire of anger. Their source, the eternal fountain, is God.

A difficult passage. Virgil did not ask out of ignorance, like someone who sees only with the body's eyes and so cannot tell what is happening to a person lying senseless. He asked to get Dante moving again.
The Italian word is "vespero", the last quarter of the day. The sun is still above the horizon, low and bright in the travelers' faces.
The penance of the wrathful. Anger blinds the mind and chokes the breath like smoke. The souls of this terrace walk in a darkness as thick as the one their rage once made in them (Canto 16).
